headline: Basecamp values craft, calm work, and long-term stability over growth hype and always has.
identity: Basecamp has consistently valued craft, simplicity, and treating people right—qualities that have remained remarkably stable across its 17-year public presence. The company's language around altruism and belonging strengthened notably from 2020–2022 (peaking in 2021–2022 with language about shared values and inclusive hiring), but has since moderated back toward mission-focused framing by 2024–2026. Craft language, once a signature strength (zscore 1.45 in 2009), has declined sharply since 2019, dropping to negative zscores by 2023–2026—a shift reflecting a move away from product-focused hiring copy toward operational and decision-making philosophy.
fit: You might be a good fit if you are self-directed, intellectually curious, and comfortable working asynchronously across time zones without constant real-time communication. The company explicitly seeks 'managers of one'—people who set their own direction and thrive in calm, low-distraction environments. You should also value long-term stability and meaningful work over rapid growth or status climbing.

sections.heading: A stable core: simplicity, craft, and treating people right
sections.body:
From 2009 onward, Basecamp's careers copy has anchored itself in three commitments: quality and simplicity in products, care for customers and employees, and profitable independence. Quotes like 'Quality, clarity, attention to detail, and usefulness are at the core of everything we do' (2009) and 'Treating people right is fundamental to how we do business' (2014–2021) appear consistently across the years. The company's altruism language remained below-average relative to peers through 2018 (zscore –0.53), then rose sharply in 2020–2022 (peaking at zscore 1.48 in 2021), driven by explicit language about shared values, long-term careers, and responsibility to customers. By 2024–2026, altruism language settled back to moderate levels (zscore 0.42–0.67), suggesting the company moved past a period of values-heavy messaging and returned to more operational framing.

Craft language—emphasis on doing excellent work, attention to detail, and building products that last—was a defining strength in 2009–2017 (zscores 0.97–1.59), but has declined sharply since 2019. By 2023–2026, craft zscores turned negative (–1.11 to –1.28), indicating the careers copy shifted away from product excellence and toward process, decision-making, and team dynamics. This reflects a maturation: the company no longer needs to recruit on the promise of 'building great software' but instead on the promise of 'working in a calm, well-organized system.'

sections.heading: Wellbeing and async work: a growing emphasis since 2019
sections.body: Basecamp's language around wellbeing—rest, focus, asynchronous communication, and freedom from interruption—has grown substantially since 2019. Wellbeing zscores were negative or flat through 2018 (–0.09 to 0.30), but jumped to 1.38 in 2019 and remained elevated through 2022 (zscores 0.60–1.19). Quotes like 'Having a chat room where you can just say good morning, let people know you're out for lunch, and generally just feel part of something is a powerful counter to cabin fever' (2019) and 'Set expectations that it's OK to be unavailable' (2021) became central to the pitch. This shift coincides with the company's public critique of Slack and group chat (launched in 2019 on the careers site), positioning Basecamp as a refuge from always-on culture. By 2024–2026, wellbeing language remained elevated but moderated slightly, suggesting the company has integrated async-first work as a baseline expectation rather than a novel selling point.

sections.heading: Inclusion and meritocracy: a brief surge, then rebalancing
sections.body: Inclusion language (diversity, belonging, welcoming different perspectives) was nearly absent in 2009–2015, then spiked in 2017 (zscore 1.49) with language like 'You hear a lot of talk from tech companies that diversity is important for making great software. 100% true, but diversity has deeper value beyond monetary.' Inclusion remained elevated through 2022 (zscore 1.87), but dropped sharply by 2025–2026 (zscore –1.63 to –1.94), the lowest in the dataset. Meritocracy language followed a similar arc: weak in 2009–2018, then strong in 2021–2022 (zscores 0.43–2.04), with explicit statements like 'We don't place independent value on where you come from, where you live, where you worked before, where you went to school' (2022). By 2024–2026, meritocracy language also declined (zscores 0.61 to –1.97). This suggests the company moved through a period of explicit DEI messaging (2017–2022) and has since returned to a more neutral, process-focused tone that emphasizes capability and fit over demographic representation.

sections.heading: Performance and autonomy: consistent, with a recent shift toward decision-making
sections.body: Performance language (doing great work, excellence, high standards) has remained relatively stable and positive across the entire period (zscores –0.84 to 2.10), peaking in 2017 and 2022. However, the *framing* of performance has shifted. Early years (2009–2018) emphasized 'building the best product' and 'doing exceptional work.' By 2019–2026, performance language increasingly focused on autonomy, self-management, and decision-making: 'People who do this well are managers of one, and we expect everyone to embody this principle' (2022–2024). The 2025–2026 careers copy introduced a new emphasis on decision-making philosophy ('The 37signals Guide to Making Decisions'), suggesting the company is now recruiting on the basis of judgment and independence rather than raw output or product ambition.
